stories.bridge: 1968 named the crisis; the discipline has been answering it ever since. Now let's build the technical depth that lets you lead engineers — starting with the craft itself.
stories.hook: In October 1968, NATO convened an emergency conference in a Bavarian village: software was in crisis, and no one knew how to build it reliably.
stories.narrative: The setting was Garmisch, Germany, and the attendees — Edsger Dijkstra, Tony Hoare, John Naur, and dozens more — had been summoned by the NATO Science Committee to confront what everyone was calling the software crisis: projects late, over budget, and buggy, with no engineering discipline to fix it. The conference's deliberate provocation was in its title: 'Software Engineering.' The phrase was chosen to be aspirational, even ironic — software was manifestly not yet an engineering discipline, and calling it one was a challenge. The report that emerged, edited by Peter Naur and Brian Randell, diagnosed the disease: software was built by craft and heroism, without the measurement, specification, and management methods that other engineering fields took for granted. Out of Garmisch came the next decade's agenda — structured programming, formal methods, project management — and the term stuck so thoroughly that we forget it was invented as a dare. For the technical leader, the 1968 story is the founding myth with a live moral: the gap between 'programming' and 'engineering' is process, measurement, and accountability, and closing it is the TPM's job. When interviewers probe your technical depth, they're checking whether you can operate on both sides of that gap — deep enough in the craft to earn engineers' respect, disciplined enough in process to ship. The village was Garmisch. The dare is permanent. The Garmisch report's recommendations — better specification, measurement, and management — became the next two decades' research agenda, from structured programming to formal methods. The irony the industry still lives with: software did become an engineering discipline, but the craft never fully surrendered to the process. The TPM's job, then and now, is the balance Garmisch named — enough process to ship reliably, enough craft to solve the unknown. Your interview answers should show you can hold both.
stories.title: The story behind the term 'software engineering'
verifiedClaims: The NATO Software Engineering conference was held in Garmisch, Germany, in October 1968
The term was deliberately provocative; attendees included Dijkstra, Hoare, and Naur

stories.bridge: Grove's discipline turned goals into a system. Now let's learn metrics and judgment — the TPM/PM skill of choosing what to measure and what the numbers mean.

figures.name: Andy Grove
figures.role: CEO of Intel; created the OKR discipline

figures.name: John Doerr
figures.role: Venture capitalist; brought OKRs to Google in 1999

stories.hook: In the 1970s, Andy Grove ran Intel on a simple discipline: objectives, key results, scored quarterly — no hiding.
stories.narrative: Grove, the Hungarian émigré who became Intel's legendary CEO, believed that management was an engineering problem: outputs could be measured, processes could be tuned, and vague goals were a form of lying. His system, which he called iMBOs — Intel Management by Objectives — required every team to set a qualitative objective and a handful of quantitative key results, then score them honestly each quarter: 1.0 meant done, 0.7 was often the target for stretch goals, and anything fudged was a cultural failure. He codified the philosophy in 'High Output Management' (1983), one of the most influential management books ever written. In 1999, the venture capitalist John Doerr — who had learned the system at Intel — carried it to a young Google, presenting it to Larry Page, Sergey Brin, and thirty employees; he called them OKRs, Objectives and Key Results. Google ran on OKRs from that day forward, and the discipline spread through Silicon Valley like a protocol: set the objective, define the measurable results, score without mercy, learn. Doerr later wrote 'Measure What Matters' (2018) to document the spread. For the leadership interview, OKRs are the canonical answer to 'how do you align a team': the method forces the two skills this module teaches — choosing the right metrics (judgment) and reading them honestly (discipline). Grove's rule was that the score is a tool for learning, not a weapon for review. Teams that forget that get theater; teams that remember it get focus. The scoring discipline is what most companies get wrong: Grove insisted that a 0.7 on a stretch goal beats a 1.0 on a safe one, because the point is ambition, not compliance. Teams that tie OKRs to compensation get sandbagging; teams that tie them to learning get honesty. In your leadership interviews, the OKR story signals that you understand metrics as instruments of alignment, not surveillance — the distinction this module's judgment training is built on.
stories.title: The story behind OKRs
verifiedClaims: Grove developed the system at Intel in the 1970s; 'High Output Management' was published in 1983
Doerr introduced OKRs to Google in 1999
Doerr documented the spread in 'Measure What Matters' (2018)

stories.bridge: The scrum is rugby's restart — messy, collective, forward-moving. Now let's learn the execution engine: how leaders turn plans into shipped software.
stories.hook: In 1995, Jeff Sutherland and Ken Schwaber named a software process after a rugby formation.
stories.narrative: Sutherland, a former Air Force pilot who had flown in Vietnam, and Schwaber, a consultant, had been experimenting with faster, more adaptive ways to build software — Sutherland at Easel Corporation in the early 1990s, where the first 'scrum' ran. They borrowed the metaphor from a 1986 Harvard Business Review article by Hirotaka Takeuchi and Ikujiro Nonaka, 'The New New Product Development Game,' which had compared high-performing product teams to a rugby scrum: the whole pack moving together down the field, passing the ball back and forth, adapting in real time — versus the relay-race model of specialists handing off in sequence. Sutherland and Schwaber formalized the practice in a 1995 OOPSLA paper and spent the next decade spreading it: fixed-length sprints, a prioritized backlog, daily stand-ups, the retrospective — rituals designed to make progress visible and adaptation cheap. Scrum became the default rhythm of software teams worldwide, for better and worse: at its best, a team that inspects and adapts; at its worst, theater. For the leadership interview, the execution questions — 'tell me about a project that slipped,' 'how do you run a team' — are really questions about whether you understand what the rituals are for. The scrum isn't the stand-up; it's the principle underneath: small batches, fast feedback, and a team that owns its process. Sutherland learned it flying jets, where the OODA loop is life and death. Your sprints are lower-stakes, but the loop is the same: observe, orient, decide, act — every two weeks, without fail. The rituals ossified into certification industries, and Sutherland himself has warned against the cargo cult — stand-ups without inspection, sprints without adaptation. The 1995 paper's actual claim was modest: empirical process control beats defined process for complex work. Keep that sentence in your pocket for interviews: when they ask how you run teams, the answer is the principle, not the rituals.
stories.title: The story behind Scrum
verifiedClaims: Sutherland and Schwaber presented Scrum at OOPSLA in 1995
The rugby metaphor comes from Takeuchi and Nonaka's 1986 HBR article
Sutherland first ran it at Easel Corporation in the early 1990s
